title: Postdiagnosis body fatness, weight change and breast cancer prognosis: Global Cancer Update Program (CUP global) systematic literature review and meta‐analysis

subsections.subsection_title: Global Burden of Obesity and Relevance to Breast Cancer
subsections.content:
Obesity has become a defining global public-health challenge. Pooled analyses of measured anthropometry show a sustained rise in body-mass index (BMI) across most world regions since the late twentieth century, with particularly steep increases in many low- and middle-income settings, even where undernutrition persists alongside excess adiposity ref [1], ref [2], ref [3]. This worldwide shift reflects profound changes in food systems, urbanization, sedentary occupations, and the commercial availability of energy-dense diets, producing a true double burden of malnutrition rather than a simple replacement of underweight by obesity ref [1], ref [4], ref [5].

These secular trends are directly relevant to breast cancer because excess body fatness is now highly prevalent among women at the ages when breast cancer incidence is greatest. Global cancer surveillance consistently identifies breast cancer as the most commonly diagnosed cancer in women worldwide, and obesity is increasingly recognized as an important modifiable determinant of both cancer burden and survivorship needs ref [6], ref [7], ref [8]. The association is strongest for postmenopausal breast cancer, for which higher BMI and adult weight gain are linked to increased incidence in large pooled and prospective studies ref [9], ref [10], ref [11], ref [12]. In premenopausal disease, associations are more heterogeneous, but obesity remains clinically important because it shapes comorbidity, tumor detection, treatment delivery, and later outcomes ref [11], ref [13], ref [14].

From a population perspective, the convergence of rising obesity prevalence and the growing global burden of breast cancer implies that adiposity will influence an increasing fraction of diagnoses and downstream prognosis. Biological pathways connecting obesity to breast carcinogenesis include higher circulating estrogens after menopause, hyperinsulinemia, insulin-like growth factor signaling, chronic low-grade inflammation, and adipokine dysregulation ref [15], ref [16], ref [17], ref [18]. These mechanisms also provide the rationale for studying postdiagnosis body fatness and weight change as prognostic factors, particularly as more women are living longer after breast cancer diagnosis in settings where obesity prevalence remains high ref [7], ref [19], ref [20], ref [21].

subsections.subsection_title: Adiposity, Physical Activity, and Breast Cancer Risk
subsections.content:
Adiposity and physical activity are among the best-studied modifiable determinants of breast cancer risk, but their effects vary across the life course and by menopausal status. The WCRF Continuous Update Project, synthesizing 126 cohort studies, concluded that higher physical activity is associated with lower risk of both premenopausal and postmenopausal breast cancer, whereas greater adult adiposity and weight gain increase risk primarily after menopause; in contrast, higher early-adult BMI shows an inverse association with risk before and after menopause ref [2].

The postmenopausal association appears especially robust for hormone receptor-positive disease and is weaker among current users of menopausal hormone therapy, supporting an estrogen-mediated mechanism in which adipose tissue becomes a major source of aromatization after menopause ref [2]. Measures of central adiposity, including waist circumference and waist-to-hip ratio, also show positive associations with postmenopausal breast cancer, although attenuation after BMI adjustment suggests overlap between total and abdominal fatness rather than wholly independent effects ref [2]. Umbrella-level evidence further classifies the association of adult weight gain with postmenopausal breast cancer in never-users of hormone replacement therapy as among the strongest adiposity-cancer relationships across major cancer sites ref [3].

Physical activity likely influences risk through both weight-dependent and weight-independent pathways, including reductions in insulin resistance, chronic inflammation, and circulating estrogens. Conversely, sedentary behavior may confer additional risk, with prolonged sitting associated with higher postmenopausal breast cancer incidence in the WCRF review ref [2]. Collectively, this literature frames breast cancer etiology within an energy-balance model in which long-term adiposity, fat distribution, and habitual movement jointly shape risk.

subsections.subsection_title: Obesity in Breast Cancer Diagnosis, Treatment, and Prognosis
subsections.content:
Obesity complicates the breast cancer pathway from diagnosis onward. Compared with normal-weight women, those with obesity are less likely to adhere to mammographic screening, report more pain and embarrassment during screening, and may therefore present with larger or more advanced tumors despite similar mammographic sensitivity across body-size groups ref [4], ref [3], ref [4], ref [2]. These diagnostic delays intersect with socioeconomic disadvantage and weight stigma, which can further reduce engagement with preventive and oncologic care ref [5], ref [6], ref [7].

During local treatment, obesity is consistently associated with higher perioperative risk, including anesthesia-related difficulty, wound complications after mastectomy, and lower sentinel lymph node identification rates ref [2], ref [8], ref [9], ref [10]. Obese patients are also more likely to experience poorer cosmetic outcomes after breast-conserving therapy and substantially higher complication and reoperation rates after reconstruction ref [11], ref [12], ref [13], ref [14]. In radiotherapy, larger body habitus and breast volume can worsen dose inhomogeneity and acute skin toxicity, while obesity also increases the risk of treatment-related lymphedema ref [15], ref [16], ref [17].

Prognostically, obesity is linked to inferior disease-free, breast cancer-specific, and overall survival, even when standard local and systemic therapies are delivered ref [18], ref [19], ref [2]. Chemotherapy underdosing has historically contributed to concern, prompting guideline recommendations to use full weight-based dosing in obese adults ref [20], ref [21]. Yet adverse outcomes persist beyond dosing alone: cohort and trial data suggest reduced benefit from adjuvant therapy, including poorer outcomes with endocrine treatment in heavier women and possible attenuation of aromatase inhibitor efficacy relative to tamoxifen ref [19], ref [22], ref [23]. Collectively, these findings support obesity as both a treatment-modifying factor and an independent marker of worse breast cancer prognosis.

subsections.subsection_title: Metabolic Effects of Breast Cancer Therapy
subsections.content:
Breast cancer therapy can itself perturb systemic metabolism, with effects extending beyond short-term toxicities. A systematic review of adjuvant chemotherapy and aromatase inhibitors found a consistent overall pattern of rising fasting glucose, insulin, and insulin resistance indices, although the underlying studies were small and methodologically heterogeneous ref [5]. Prospective and retrospective cohorts similarly report increases in metabolic syndrome components, HbA1c, insulin, or HOMA-IR during or after adjuvant treatment, supporting the view that therapy may accelerate pre-existing metabolic vulnerability in survivors ref [2], ref [3], ref [4], ref [5], ref [6].

Several mechanisms likely contribute. Classic studies linked adjuvant chemotherapy to weight gain and reduced resting energy expenditure, while later work showed that treatment-related weight change often reflects increased fat mass with loss of lean tissue rather than simple overall weight accrual ref [7], ref [8], ref [9]. Contemporary reviews emphasize sarcopenic obesity, fatigue, reduced physical activity, altered appetite, glucocorticoid exposure, and inflammatory signaling as plausible drivers of insulin resistance during treatment ref [10], ref [11]. Observational evidence also suggests that metabolic disruption may persist, with breast cancer survivors showing elevated risks of incident diabetes after chemotherapy or endocrine therapy in some cohorts ref [12], ref [13].

Endocrine therapy introduces an additional layer of metabolic complexity. Aromatase inhibitors, through profound estrogen deprivation, have been associated with less favorable lipid and cardiovascular profiles than tamoxifen, whereas tamoxifen may differentially affect adiposity and hepatic fat distribution ref [14], ref [15], ref [16]. Emerging data further indicate that aromatase inhibitor exposure may modify adipokines and body composition, and genetic susceptibility may shape these responses ref [17], ref [18]. Collectively, these findings frame postdiagnosis adiposity and weight change not merely as behavioral sequelae of treatment, but as biologically entangled consequences of breast cancer therapy with potential relevance for recurrence, cardiovascular disease, and long-term survival ref [5], ref [10], ref [19].

Meta-analyses on postdiagnosis adiposity and breast cancer prognosis typically rely on random-effects pooling to accommodate between-study variability in exposure definition, timing of weight ascertainment, menopausal status, treatment era, and outcome ascertainment. In this setting, inverse-variance random-effects models derived from the DerSimonian-Laird framework remain common, although their limitations under substantial heterogeneity and small numbers of studies are well recognized; extensions to multivariate random-effects meta-analysis are especially relevant when multiple correlated prognostic endpoints or adiposity metrics are synthesized jointly ref [8].

For continuous BMI and adiposity analyses, dose-response methods are particularly important because categorization into normal weight, overweight, and obesity can obscure threshold or nonlinear associations. Two-stage generalized least-squares trend estimation and flexible nonlinear meta-analysis using restricted cubic splines provide a principled way to reconstruct study-specific slopes from published category-specific risk estimates while accounting for within-study covariance among log-risk estimates ref [9]. These methods are preferable to naive trend models that assume independence across categories, which can bias standard errors and heterogeneity tests ref [9].

Bias appraisal in this literature should go beyond pooled point estimates. Small-study effects are commonly explored with funnel plots and Egger-type regression tests, but asymmetry must be interpreted cautiously because it may reflect true heterogeneity, selective reporting, exposure misclassification, or sparse-study artifacts rather than publication bias alone ref [6]. Leave-one-out analyses, studentized deleted residuals, Cook's distance, DFBETAS, and covariance-ratio diagnostics are useful for identifying influential cohorts or outlying contrasts, particularly when a few large studies dominate pooled hazard ratios ref [7].

Accordingly, rigorous evidence appraisal for observational prognosis meta-analyses should integrate heterogeneity quantification, nonlinear trend modeling, influence diagnostics, and structured risk-of-bias assessment for confounding, reverse causation, and selective reporting. These methodological safeguards are essential when interpreting associations between postdiagnosis BMI, weight change, and breast cancer outcomes, where modest relative risks can be highly sensitive to modeling assumptions and study quality ref [6], ref [7], ref [8], ref [9].

subsections.subsection_title: Observational Evidence on BMI, Obesity, and Breast Cancer Prognosis
subsections.content:
Observational cohort evidence generally associates higher BMI or obesity at diagnosis with poorer breast cancer prognosis, although effect sizes and consistency vary by age, menopausal status, disease subtype, and treatment context. Several cohorts reported that obese patients present with larger tumors, greater nodal involvement, and other adverse clinicopathologic features, which may partly mediate inferior outcomes ref [11], ref [14], ref [8], ref [12], ref [13]. In the large Danish early-stage cohort, obesity independently predicted distant metastasis and breast cancer death after adjustment, with little effect on locoregional recurrence, and the adverse association became more evident beyond 5-10 years of follow-up ref [14].

Evidence in younger and predominantly premenopausal populations also supports a prognostic role for obesity. In the UK POSH cohort, obesity at diagnosis was associated with larger tumors, more node-positive and grade 3 disease, more triple-negative tumors, and worse distant disease-free interval and overall survival; adjusted effects were strongest in ER-positive disease ref [11]. Earlier Australian data similarly found obesity independently associated with recurrence and all-cause mortality, including among premenopausal women ref [8]. By contrast, some institutional or regional series observed worse presentation but null or weak survival associations, underscoring heterogeneity related to sample size, BMI ascertainment, and residual confounding ref [10], ref [13], ref [15].

Recent data from non-Western and population-based settings are broadly compatible with this pattern but remain mixed. A Jordanian institutional study linked obesity to higher grade, worse composite prognostic scores, and roughly two-fold higher odds of recurrence, particularly in postmenopausal patients ref [12]. Conversely, a New Zealand population-based cohort of chemotherapy-treated patients found no clear association of postdiagnosis BMI with breast cancer-specific or overall mortality after multivariable adjustment ref [15]. Taken together, the observational literature supports obesity as a marker—and in many cohorts an independent correlate—of poorer prognosis, while emphasizing effect modification by menopausal status, ER biology, timing of BMI assessment, and treatment delivery ref [11], ref [14], ref [8], ref [15].

subsections.subsection_title: Treatment Response, Toxicity, and Therapy-Specific Effects
subsections.content:
Evidence on treatment response suggests that adiposity may differentially affect neoadjuvant chemotherapy efficacy. In a retrospective series of locally advanced breast cancer treated with doxorubicin-docetaxel, obesity was associated with a lower likelihood of achieving a broader pathological response endpoint (pCR1) and with shorter overall survival, although estimates were imprecise because of limited sample size ref [18]. Similar signals were reported in a Saudi multicenter cohort, in which overweight/obesity was the only independent factor inversely associated with pathologic complete response after anthracycline-taxane neoadjuvant therapy ref [5]. Together, these studies support the view that excess adiposity may reduce chemosensitivity or reflect treatment-related undertreatment and altered pharmacokinetics in the neoadjuvant setting ref [18], ref [5].

Therapy-specific effects are also evident for endocrine treatment. In the prospective ABCSG-12 analysis, body mass index modified outcomes among premenopausal women receiving ovarian suppression: overweight/obese patients treated with anastrozole plus goserelin had higher risks of recurrence and death than normal-weight patients, whereas BMI had little prognostic impact in the tamoxifen arm ref [19]. These findings are consistent with the hypothesis that greater aromatase substrate availability, or incomplete ovarian suppression in heavier patients, may attenuate aromatase-inhibitor efficacy ref [19].

Toxicity data indicate that obesity can amplify adverse-event burden under intensive chemotherapy schedules. In the randomized GAIN study, obese patients receiving dose-dense chemotherapy according to actual body surface area had higher rates of febrile neutropenia, grade 3/4 thrombocytopenia, and thromboembolic events than obese patients treated with adjusted dosing, yet disease-free and overall survival were not improved by full dosing ref [17]. This observation is notable because it contrasts with the broader ASCO principle of full weight-based dosing in most curative settings, suggesting that highly dose-dense regimens may require more nuanced consideration than standard schedules ref [17]. Overall, the literature points to heterogeneous, regimen-dependent effects of adiposity on response, toxicity, and endocrine sensitivity rather than a uniform prognostic mechanism.

Evidence on postdiagnosis weight change suggests that dynamic weight trajectories may be prognostically relevant, but the observational literature remains methodologically heterogeneous. In a long-term French cohort treated with anthracycline-based chemotherapy, weight change exceeding 5% in either direction during treatment was associated with poorer disease-free and overall survival, with multivariable relative risks of 2.28 for recurrence and 2.11 for death versus weight stability ref [21]. This study is notable because it examined both gain and loss as potentially adverse departures from metabolic stability rather than focusing only on weight gain ref [21].

Even so, causal interpretation is limited. Weight loss during therapy may partly reflect occult disease burden, treatment intolerance, sarcopenia, or systemic inflammation rather than a modifiable exposure per se, while weight gain may capture reduced activity, corticosteroid exposure, menopause, and unfavorable body-composition change despite modest scale-weight shifts ref [21]. Thus, weight change should be viewed as a composite clinical signal that may index vulnerability, treatment effects, and adiposity-related biology simultaneously.

Intervention evidence is much thinner than observational evidence. The LISA randomized trial tested a 2-year telephone-based diet and physical-activity program in postmenopausal hormone receptor-positive patients on letrozole and achieved greater weight loss than education alone at 6 to 24 months, but the between-arm difference was not sustained long term ref [22]. Because accrual stopped early, the trial was underpowered for prognosis; nevertheless, disease-free survival numerically favored intervention (HR 0.71, 95% CI 0.41-1.24), while overall survival showed no clear effect ref [22]. Taken together, current evidence supports monitoring weight trajectories during treatment and survivorship, but does not yet establish that intentional postdiagnosis weight loss improves breast cancer outcomes.

subsections.subsection_title: Related Survivorship and Special Clinical Contexts
subsections.content:
A related survivorship issue is the risk of second primary cancers after breast cancer, which becomes increasingly relevant as survival improves. In a nested case–control study of breast cancer survivors, obesity emerged as one of the strongest predictors of second primary tumours, alongside smoking, hypertension, family history of non-breast cancer, and longer survival time, whereas treatment variables were comparatively weaker predictors overall ref [2]. This observation is consistent with broader survivorship epidemiology showing elevated incidence of second malignancies after breast cancer and the contribution of both shared host factors and prior therapy exposures ref [3], ref [4], ref [5].

The second-cancer pattern is clinically heterogeneous. Gynecologic malignancies, particularly endometrial cancer, have been linked to tamoxifen exposure, while radiotherapy and selected chemotherapy regimens have been associated with later risks of lung cancer, sarcoma, and hematologic neoplasms, often with long latency ref [6], ref [7], ref [8], ref [9]. At the same time, registry-based studies suggest that lifestyle-related factors such as excess adiposity and smoking may rival or exceed treatment effects in some settings, reinforcing the importance of long-term risk-factor management in survivorship care ref [2], ref [10].

Special clinical contexts also include hereditary susceptibility and younger survivors, in whom family history and germline predisposition may shape both prognosis and risk of additional primaries ref [11], ref [12]. Overall, these data extend the prognosis discussion beyond recurrence and breast-cancer-specific mortality: postdiagnosis body fatness may influence not only breast cancer outcomes but also competing and subsequent cancer events, supporting integrated surveillance, cardiometabolic prevention, smoking cessation, and weight management within survivorship programs ref [2], ref [13].

subsections.section_title: Results of the Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
subsections.content:
Evidence synthesized in the CUP Global review indicates that higher baseline adiposity at or near diagnosis is generally associated with poorer prognosis after breast cancer, particularly for overall and breast-cancer-specific mortality. This pattern is consistent with older observational literature and remains biologically plausible through endocrine, inflammatory, and insulin-related pathways that may promote progression and competing cardiometabolic mortality [ref 1, ref 2].

The adverse association is not restricted to BMI alone. In a population-based cohort of women aged 20–54 years, obesity at interview was associated with higher all-cause mortality versus ideal weight (HR 1.48, 95% CI 1.09–2.01), and central adiposity showed a similar gradient: the highest versus lowest waist-to-hip ratio quartile yielded an HR of 1.52 (95% CI 1.05–2.19) [ref 1]. Notably, women who were overweight/obese both at age 20 and near diagnosis had substantially worse survival (HR 2.22, 95% CI 1.45–3.40), suggesting that duration of adiposity exposure may matter in addition to absolute BMI [ref 1].

Complementing these findings, Nichols et al. reported in nearly 4,000 nonmetastatic survivors that prediagnosis obesity was associated with increased all-cause mortality (HR 1.52, 95% CI 1.17–1.98) and cardiovascular mortality (HR 2.45, 95% CI 1.46–4.11) relative to normal BMI; postdiagnosis obesity was also associated with higher breast-cancer-specific mortality (HR 2.28, 95% CI 1.43–3.64) [ref 2]. Together, these studies reinforce that both general and abdominal adiposity at baseline are clinically relevant prognostic markers, while also highlighting that part of the excess risk may arise through non-cancer deaths, especially cardiovascular disease [ref 1, ref 2].

subsections.section_title: Results of the Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
subsections.content:
Evidence on post-diagnosis weight change indicates that prognosis is generally most favorable among women who remain relatively weight stable, whereas both weight loss and substantial weight gain tend to be associated with poorer outcomes. In the After Breast Cancer Pooling Project, encompassing 12,915 stage I–III survivors from U.S. and Shanghai cohorts, the association with overall mortality was U-shaped: large weight loss (≥10%) was associated with higher mortality in both settings, while large weight gain showed a weaker adverse pattern, particularly in U.S. cohorts ref [5]. Similar conclusions emerged from the Chicago multiethnic cohort, where longitudinal BMI trajectories showed a nonlinear association with survival, with BMI loss >0.5 kg/m2/year strongly associated with overall, breast cancer-specific, and disease-free mortality, and BMI gain showing a smaller but still unfavorable association ref [27].

Across individual cohort studies, weight loss has been the most consistent adverse signal. In the Long Island cohort, women who lost >5% of prediagnosis weight had markedly elevated all-cause and breast cancer-specific mortality, while gain >10% was also associated with worse survival ref [4]. In the pooled ABCPP analysis, the excess risk associated with weight loss appeared modified by baseline BMI and comorbidity, with higher mortality especially evident among U.S. women with comorbid conditions and among leaner women in both U.S. and Shanghai cohorts ref [5]. The Chicago study further suggested that substantial weight loss often began well before death, raising the possibility that at least part of the observed association reflects occult disease progression, cachexia, or worsening comorbidity rather than a purely causal effect of weight loss itself ref [27].

Overall, the literature supports a cautious interpretation: post-diagnosis weight loss is reproducibly associated with worse prognosis, whereas the evidence for weight gain is weaker and more heterogeneous, tending to emerge for larger gains or in specific subgroups ref [4], ref [5], ref [27]. These patterns underscore an important methodological limitation of observational studies—most cannot distinguish intentional from unintentional weight change. Accordingly, while prevention of excessive gain remains reasonable, involuntary weight loss after diagnosis should be regarded as a potential clinical warning sign warranting evaluation for recurrence, treatment toxicity, sarcopenia, or comorbidity burden ref [27], ref [5].

subsections.section_title: Results of the Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
subsections.content:
Evidence on weight change specifically during systemic therapy is limited and heterogeneous, but the available studies suggest that treatment-period weight trajectories may carry prognostic information that is not fully captured by baseline adiposity alone. In the adjuvant setting, a large retrospective cohort of 1,998 women receiving third-generation chemotherapy found that weight change during treatment was common in both directions and was largely transient, with many patients trending back toward baseline by 1 year after chemotherapy; importantly, chemotherapy-related BMI gain was not clearly associated with overall survival or distant recurrence, although a modest association with locoregional recurrence was reported [1].

Data from neoadjuvant cohorts are less consistent. In Chinese patients with operable stage II–III disease, BMI increased modestly during neoadjuvant chemotherapy, and a gain >2 kg/m2 was independently associated with poorer disease-free survival and overall survival, while showing no relation to pathologic complete response [2]. By contrast, in a larger MD Anderson cohort of locally advanced breast cancer, BMI increase during neoadjuvant treatment was not an independent predictor of recurrence-free or overall survival overall, and subgroup analyses even suggested higher pathologic complete response rates among normal-weight/underweight or postmenopausal women with increasing BMI [3]. These conflicting findings likely reflect differences in disease stage, treatment duration, menopausal composition, follow-up, and definitions of weight change [1-3].

Taken together, the CUP Global evidence indicates that weight change during systemic therapy should not be interpreted simplistically as uniformly harmful. Short-term gains during adjuvant chemotherapy may be transient and of limited prognostic relevance, whereas larger gains during neoadjuvant treatment in some cohorts appear to mark worse subsequent outcomes [1,2]. The inconsistency across studies underscores the need for standardized exposure definitions, repeated body-composition assessment beyond BMI alone, and analyses that distinguish intentional from treatment-related weight change [1-3].

subsections.subsection_title: Prognostic Significance of Adiposity in Early and Metastatic Breast Cancer
subsections.content:
Across early breast cancer cohorts, higher adiposity is generally associated with poorer prognosis, although the effect is not uniform across endpoints or subtypes. Large registry and trial-based analyses consistently report worse overall survival, and often worse distant recurrence, among women with obesity at diagnosis, even after adjustment for stage and treatment factors ref [32], ref [8], ref [12], ref [13]. Notably, the Danish Breast Cancer Cooperative Group analysis found obesity to be independently associated with a higher risk of distant metastasis and breast-cancer death, while not materially affecting locoregional recurrence, suggesting that adiposity may be more closely linked to systemic progression than to local failure ref [32].

Important heterogeneity emerges by biology. In operable disease, obesity appears especially detrimental in hormone receptor-positive/HER2-negative tumors, where ECOG analyses showed significantly inferior disease-free, overall, and breast cancer-specific survival, whereas analogous associations were not evident in triple-negative or HER2-positive subsets ref [33]. Earlier International Breast Cancer Study Group data likewise suggested a stronger adverse effect on overall survival than on disease-free survival, particularly among pre/perimenopausal women treated with chemotherapy alone ref [8]. By contrast, pooled analyses in anthracycline/taxane-treated populations indicate that the risk may concentrate at the upper extreme of BMI, with severe obesity rather than modest obesity driving recurrence and mortality, and with less clear variation by pathological subtype ref [12], ref [13]. In HER2-positive early disease, contemporary pooled trial data also support worse survival with overweight and obesity ref [35].

The metastatic setting is more complex and less consistent. In one pooled cohort of patients receiving first-line chemotherapy for metastatic breast cancer, BMI was not independently associated with progression-free or overall survival ref [10]. However, more recent pooled analyses restricted to HER2-positive advanced disease reported the opposite pattern, with overweight and obesity associated with improved progression-free and overall survival, an observation framed as an 'obesity paradox' ref [35]. Taken together, the literature supports adiposity as an adverse prognostic marker in early breast cancer—especially for distant outcomes and in endocrine-responsive disease—while in metastatic disease its prognostic meaning appears context-dependent and may vary by subtype, treatment line, and host reserve ref [32], ref [33], ref [35], ref [10].

subsections.subsection_title: Interaction of Obesity with Systemic Therapy Efficacy
subsections.content:
Evidence that adiposity modifies systemic therapy efficacy is most developed for endocrine therapy. In premenopausal hormone receptor–positive disease, the ABCSG-12 analysis suggested that overweight women receiving goserelin plus anastrozole had higher risks of recurrence and death than normal-weight women, whereas this pattern was not seen with tamoxifen, raising concern that aromatase inhibition and/or ovarian suppression may be less complete in women with greater adiposity ref [19]. In postmenopausal disease, the ATAC exploratory analysis similarly reported that recurrence rates remained lower with anastrozole than tamoxifen overall, but the relative advantage appeared greater in leaner women, consistent with the hypothesis that excess adipose aromatase activity could attenuate AI efficacy ref [7].

However, this interaction is not uniform across endocrine agents or trials. In NSABP B-14, obesity was not associated with diminished tamoxifen benefit for recurrence or breast cancer mortality in node-negative ER-positive disease, although obesity increased contralateral breast cancer, other second cancers, and all-cause mortality ref [40]. Likewise, in BIG 1-98, baseline BMI showed no significant treatment-by-BMI interaction for letrozole versus tamoxifen; letrozole retained superiority across BMI strata, suggesting that the more potent estrogen suppression achieved by letrozole may overcome the attenuation proposed for anastrozole ref [41]. Taken together, these data argue against a simple class effect and instead support drug-specific differences in pharmacodynamic reserve ref [41], ref [7].

For chemotherapy, emerging evidence indicates that obesity may also interact with efficacy in a regimen-dependent manner. A reanalysis of BIG 2-98 found that increasing BMI was associated with worse disease-free and overall survival specifically in the docetaxel-containing arms, but not in non-docetaxel comparators, and that this pattern persisted after restriction to patients receiving adequate relative dose intensity ref [38]. This observation is biologically plausible given the lipophilicity and distribution characteristics of taxanes, but it remains retrospective and should be interpreted cautiously until replicated. Overall, the literature suggests that obesity is not merely a prognostic host factor; in selected settings it may alter the therapeutic index of systemic treatment, particularly endocrine therapy choice and possibly taxane-based chemotherapy ref [38], ref [19], ref [41].

subsections.subsection_title: Treatment Toxicity, Dosing, and Weight Change During Care
subsections.content:
Adiposity also affects the tolerability and delivery of systemic treatment. Earlier adjuvant data suggested that obese women dosed according to actual body weight did not experience excess early hematologic or nonhematologic toxicity compared with non-obese women, while empiric dose reductions were associated with worse failure-free survival, supporting full weight-based dosing for conventional regimens ref [42]. This evidence helped shape later guidance discouraging routine dose capping in obesity, although real-world undertreatment has remained common in breast cancer care.

More recent evidence indicates that this principle may not be uniform across all regimens. In the dose-dense adjuvant GAIN trial, obese patients treated according to unadjusted body surface area had higher rates of febrile neutropenia, grade 3/4 thrombocytopenia, and thromboembolic events than obese patients whose dosing was adjusted, without clear differences in DFS or OS ref [17]. Thus, while arbitrary underdosing may compromise efficacy in standard schedules ref [42], highly dose-dense or intensified regimens may require greater nuance, particularly when obesity coexists with thrombotic risk, altered pharmacokinetics, or treatment-related metabolic vulnerability.

Weight change during care is itself clinically relevant. A meta-analysis of chemotherapy-era studies estimated a mean weight gain of about 2.7 kg during treatment, with larger gains in older CMF-based series and smaller but still meaningful increases in more contemporary regimens ref [43]. Observational cohorts further suggest that weight stability after diagnosis is associated with the most favorable outcomes, whereas large postdiagnosis weight loss is consistently linked to higher mortality and substantial weight gain may also be adverse in some groups ref [28]. Collectively, these findings argue that body weight during treatment should be monitored not merely as a lifestyle variable, but as an integrated marker of dosing adequacy, toxicity burden, comorbidity, and host resilience ref [17], ref [28], ref [43].

subsections.subsection_title: Mechanistic Interpretation: Metabolic Dysfunction and the Tumor Microenvironment
subsections.content:
Mechanistically, the adverse prognostic association of postdiagnosis adiposity in breast cancer is most plausibly mediated by obesity-related metabolic dysfunction rather than excess mass alone. Hyperinsulinemia, dysglycemia, altered adipokines, chronic low-grade inflammation, and increased peripheral sex-steroid availability converge on canonical oncogenic pathways, including PI3K/Akt/mTOR, MAPK, and JAK/STAT, thereby promoting proliferation, survival, and dissemination of residual disease ref [45], ref [46], ref [4]. In breast tumors, insulin receptor and IGF-axis signaling are widely expressed and have been linked to poorer outcomes, supporting a biologically coherent explanation for the survival gradients observed across BMI strata ref [45], ref [4].

The local adipose microenvironment further amplifies these systemic effects. Obese mammary fat is characterized by adipocyte hypertrophy, hypoxia, macrophage-rich crown-like structures, NF-kB activation, and secretion of IL-6, TNF-alpha, CCL2, leptin, and VEGF, alongside reduced adiponectin ref [46], ref [5]. This milieu can enhance aromatase activity, increase estrogen bioavailability, recruit myeloid cells, stimulate angiogenesis, and foster epithelial-mesenchymal transition and cancer stem-like phenotypes ref [46], ref [5]. Human translational studies also suggest depot-specific and peritumoral adipose signaling, with breast white adipose inflammation and adipose-tumor crosstalk associated with more aggressive local biology ref [46], ref [5].

These mechanisms likely help explain why obesity-related prognosis effects appear especially relevant in hormone receptor-positive disease, but they are not restricted to endocrine pathways. Insulin, leptin, inflammatory cytokines, and stromal remodeling may also support metastatic competence and therapeutic resistance across subtypes ref [45], ref [46], ref [4], ref [5]. A translational implication is that body size should increasingly be interpreted together with metabolic health and tumor-microenvironment markers, because these may better identify the biologic subgroup most likely to benefit from weight loss, exercise, metformin, or anti-inflammatory interventions after diagnosis ref [45], ref [46].

Methodologically, this literature is constrained by exposure misclassification and outcome inconsistency. BMI remains the dominant metric because of feasibility, but it is an imperfect surrogate for adiposity, fat distribution, sarcopenia, and the metabolic milieu most relevant to prognosis; waist measures add information, yet are less standardized across studies and populations ref [48]. Recent syntheses also show that associations differ by timing of ascertainment, outcome selected, and subtype-specific reporting, underscoring how easily pooled estimates can mix biologically distinct questions ref [8].

Outcome definition is a second major translational barrier. In early breast cancer, recurrence, disease-free survival, invasive disease-free survival, distant recurrence, and breast cancer-specific mortality are often used interchangeably despite capturing different event sets. The STEEP framework was proposed precisely to standardize these endpoints and improve cross-trial comparability and meta-analysis ref [4]. Outside trials, however, recurrence is poorly captured in routine data systems; registry-based surveillance generally lacks recurrence fields, and claims-based algorithms show only moderate validity, creating substantial potential for misclassification in real-world prognostic studies ref [5].

These issues have practical implications for translation. Future studies should incorporate repeated, preferably measured anthropometry; central adiposity and body-composition phenotypes; prespecified lag analyses to reduce reverse causation from occult disease or treatment-related wasting; and systematic reporting by stage, menopausal status, receptor subtype, and treatment intensity ref [48], ref [8]. Equally important is harmonized endpoint collection anchored to STEEP principles and better linkage of registries, pathology, electronic records, and treatment data so recurrence can be ascertained reliably in population settings ref [4], ref [5]. Only with this methodological convergence can adiposity move from a prognostic marker toward a clinically actionable stratification variable.

Declarations for reviews in this area should state funding sources, sponsor roles, author contributions, conflicts of interest, protocol registration, and data/code availability, because methodological choices materially affect pooled estimates in obesity–breast cancer prognosis research. Transparency is particularly important where outcome definitions vary across cohorts and trials, where recurrence ascertainment can be incomplete, and where treatment dosing, endocrine exposure, and subtype distributions may confound associations between postdiagnosis adiposity and prognosis [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7].

Supplementary information should therefore provide the full search strategies, eligibility decisions, risk-of-bias assessments, outcome harmonization rules, and all analytic specifications, including dose–response modeling, multivariate random-effects methods, publication-bias assessment, and influence diagnostics [8, 9, 10, 11]. Given known heterogeneity by menopausal status, tumor subtype, treatment modality, and timing/pattern of weight change, appendices should also report subgroup definitions and sensitivity analyses in detail, rather than only summary pooled estimates [12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17].

For this topic, high-value supplementary files additionally include extraction tables for BMI and weight-change categories, handling of intentional versus unintentional weight loss, adjustment sets for metabolic and treatment-related covariates, and separate presentation of all-cause, breast cancer–specific, and recurrence outcomes. Where available, protocols for interventions and survivorship cohorts can contextualize observational findings and support reproducibility and evidence updating within the CUP framework [18, 19, 20, 21, 22].
